rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds within the time limit while mapping the full retention window and revealing whether any peaks are unretained or only elute during the high-organic hold.

All peaks eluted cleanly and early, so trim the gradient window to the apparent elution window to reduce time while keeping all compounds inside the gradient. This should improve the time term without sacrificing resolution and will show whether the late peak stays in-gradient near a much lower phi1.

The broad 20 min gradient already gave full resolution, so now test a steeper version to cut analysis time and determine whether the critical mid-cluster retains acceptable resolution under compression. This directly probes how slope-sensitive the closest pairs are.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the critical mid-cluster, while 20 min fully resolves it with time penalty; 14 min is a targeted compromise near the likely optimum. This will show whether modestly reducing slope restores the 5–7 separations enough to improve CRF beyond 0.918.

The optimum appears to lie between 14 and 20 min, with pair 6/7 still slightly under-resolved at 14 min. A 16 min run should further improve that critical pair while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve a maximal time term.

Since the critical 6/7 pair is close to the resolution threshold and may not respond much further to slope alone, test a modest temperature decrease to probe selectivity changes while keeping the currently best gradient shape. This can improve a near-equal-S pair without sacrificing much run time.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing peaks 5/6, so test the opposite direction to see whether a modest temperature increase resolves the crowded mid-cluster better than 40 C. Keeping tG at 14 min preserves the current best time/resolution balance while isolating the temperature effect.

The best region is around 14–20 min at 40 C, and 16 min already gives full resolution with only a small time penalty; 18 min will map the CRF curve on the resolved side and confirm whether the optimum truly sits at 14 min or slightly longer. This also helps quantify how sharply the score falls once the critical pair is safely separated.

Since all compounds elute well before the end and the full 95% B endpoint may be unnecessarily steep, slightly narrowing the high-organic limit should shallow the gradient around the crowded mid-region without lengthening the run much. This targets improved 6/7 resolution while staying close to the current best conditions.

The slight narrowing from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF, so continue in that direction to further shallow the gradient around the critical 6/7 pair while keeping all compounds comfortably eluting within the run. This is the most direct local refinement around the current best method.

The 0.90 endpoint looks best, so now test whether a slightly steeper 12 min version can preserve enough of the improved selectivity while shortening the run and potentially maximizing CRF. This is the key tradeoff check around the current optimum window.

The first peak is still fairly early, so raising phi0 may reduce time spent below the useful elution window while keeping the favorable 0.90 endpoint and 14 min slope near the current optimum. This checks whether trimming the low-organic start improves efficiency without harming the critical mid-cluster selectivity.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF, and the first peak is still retained enough to allow one more upward step. Testing 0.15 probes whether further trimming of unused low-organic space sharpens efficiency or whether it begins to over-compress the early and critical middle peaks.

The best method so far uses phi0 0.10 and phi1 0.90; since lowering phi1 helped at phi0 0.05, test the same narrowing from the improved 0.10 start. This may further shallow the gradient in the crowded middle while keeping the favorable trimmed low-end window.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so use the remaining budget to map nearby robustness while staying on a promising ridge; increasing phi0 one more step tests whether the optimum is broad or whether early compression begins to erode resolution. This helps identify a stable backup method around the maximum.

With the maximum already achieved at 0.10/0.85/14/40, the next most informative local test is a slightly lower phi1 to define the upper edge of the optimum plateau. This checks whether the best method is exactly centered at 0.85 or whether a still narrower window can retain full resolution without introducing a time penalty.

The maximum sits in a narrow local region, and we have not yet tested the symmetric combination of the two individually favorable trims: phi0 0.15 with phi1 0.85. This checks whether slightly more front-end trimming can preserve the excellent 0.85 endpoint performance or whether 0.10 is uniquely optimal.

Both 0.15/0.85 and 0.10/0.85 are optimal, so test 0.15/0.80 to define the lower phi1 boundary of the optimum region at the improved higher phi0. This will show whether the plateau extends further or whether phi1=0.85 is the true lower limit for maximum CRF.

With the maximum already secured, use remaining injections to probe orthogonal selectivity around a faster near-optimal window; the 12 min, 40 C run mainly failed on pair 6/7, and lowering temperature can sometimes rescue a slope-compressed pair. This tests whether an alternative fast method exists through temperature/slope interplay, even though 14 min at 40 C remains the benchmark.

The maximum CRF plateau is at 14 min with phi1 0.85, so the remaining useful question is whether the 0.15/0.85 window can tolerate a slightly steeper 12 min slope better than the 0.10-start cases. This tests if extra low-end trimming supports a faster backup method while staying close to the proven optimum.

With the optimum already achieved, probe robustness of the winning window to a realistic temperature shift so you know whether the method is sensitive in routine use. The same composition at 45 C will reveal how sharply selectivity degrades around the best gradient settings.

We have seen the optimal windows are quite temperature-sensitive, so measure the lower-temperature robustness of the second max-scoring method as a final orthogonal check. This helps distinguish whether one of the two 1.000 methods is intrinsically more stable to routine temperature variation.

Use the remaining injections to finish mapping the local high-scoring region; this corner has not been tested and will define whether the optimum plateau extends to a higher phi0 when the upper endpoint is relaxed back to 0.90. It also helps confirm whether the 0.85 endpoint is truly the key factor behind the max score.

One useful remaining boundary check is whether the lower phi1 window can support a slightly longer gradient to recover any lost selectivity and potentially expose another max-scoring ridge. This complements the 14 min and 20 min results and further characterizes slope dependence near the successful 0.85 endpoint.

For the final injection, close the last untested corner of the high-scoring local region to complete the map around the optimum plateau. This confirms whether both stronger front-end trimming and a lower endpoint together remain acceptable, while the best method remains the already achieved 1.000-CRF condition.
